output.title: When metric definitions stop working
output.body:
If you run a small business, you know the moment a metric stops being useful. The count still moves, but it no longer tells you whether the work is getting better.

That usually happens when the workflow changes. A new product line, a new tool, or a small change in how people handle edge cases can make an old measure drift away from the real decision.

At that point, the choice is not “fix the metric” in the abstract. It is: do you rewrite the rule, rebuild the workflow, or keep a human override for the cases the metric cannot handle?

The practical question is simple: is the metric wrong, or is the rule wrong? If you cannot answer that, you are probably measuring the part that is easiest to count, not the part that matters.

A useful next step is to write down the actual rule in plain English and collect a few failing examples. If the workflow is repeatable and low-sensitivity, that gives you enough to see whether this is a reporting fix, a workflow redesign, or an automation candidate. Sometimes the spreadsheet is the problem. Annoying, but useful.
